source_user: A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 28: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure per-request KV growth and allocator fragmentation; check max sequence and batch; inspect active sequences; test paged/prefix cache, admission control, quantization, and context limits.
corrected_answer:
Design framing (variant 28). Treat this not as an incident to silence but as a missing capacity contract in the serving design. The system currently admits requests whose aggregate memory demand is unbounded, so the failure mode is structural.

Assumptions stated explicitly, because the priority ranking is only valid under them: single-node inference engine with a paged KV cache; static weights loaded once; CUDA caching allocator; no other tenant on the same GPUs; error is a CUDA out-of-memory from the device allocator rather than a host RSS OOM-kill. Any of these being false changes the ranking and the diagnosis must be re-derived rather than patched.

Mechanism. Steady-state GPU memory = model weights + CUDA/NCCL context and communication buffers + framework runtime buffers + activation peak of the largest scheduled batch + KV-cache pool. Only the last two scale with concurrency, which is exactly why the failure is intermittent: a deterministic sizing bug would fail on request one. KV bytes = 2 (K and V) * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * total_tokens; with GQA/MQA the kv_heads term is small, so context length and concurrent sequence count dominate, not attention-head count. If the engine preallocates a paged KV pool, genuine KV exhaustion should surface as preemption, recompute or queueing -- not as a CUDA OOM. An actual OOM therefore points outside the pool: transient activation peaks during prefill of long prompts (chunked prefill disabled or chunk size too large), caching-allocator fragmentation from mixed-size prefill buffers, or an unaccounted co-resident consumer (LoRA adapters, speculative draft model, logits/logprobs buffers proportional to batch x vocab, a second process sharing the device).

Falsifiable hypothesis H1: the OOM is driven by the un-bounded transient activation peak of concurrent prefill of long prompts, not by KV-pool capacity. Prediction: capping concurrent prefill tokens (chunked prefill with a fixed token budget, or max_num_batched_tokens set below the observed failure-time peak) eliminates OOM on a replay of the exact failing trace while the KV-pool high-water mark stays unchanged. Null result that kills H1: OOM still occurs at the same trace offset with prefill capped, or the KV high-water mark reaches 100% before the failure. Competing hypothesis H2 (allocator fragmentation): reserved-minus-allocated bytes grow monotonically over hours and OOM occurs while reserved headroom exists; discriminated by an allocator snapshot at the failure boundary and by whether expandable_segments or a periodic empty_cache changes time-to-failure.

Controlled experiment. Freeze a replayable request trace (arrival_ts, input_len, output_len) captured across the failure and record its sha256 so both arms consume byte-identical input. Two arms on the same hardware, same engine/CUDA/driver/model-config versions, one variable changed: arm A is production config, arm B caps concurrent prefill tokens. Run each arm three times to separate flakiness from effect. Primary outcome: OOM occurrences per 1000 requests. Secondary: p50/p99 TTFT, TPOT, output tokens/s, KV-block high-water mark, preemption count, and reserved-vs-allocated bytes sampled at >=1 Hz. Confounders that must be controlled or measured, not assumed away: prefix-cache hit rate differing between arms (a warm cache silently reduces prefill work and can fake a win), traffic-mix drift if replay is not used, driver-level clock throttling, and MPS/other-tenant contention.

Prioritized remediation, ordered by evidence strength and blast radius. (1) Bound the peak: enable chunked prefill and set max_num_batched_tokens plus max_num_seqs so the worst-case concurrent working set fits with explicit headroom -- this is reversible, config-only, and directly tests H1. (2) Enforce admission control: reject or queue requests whose input_len exceeds a declared max_model_len rather than letting them into the batch; an unbounded context limit is a capacity contract that was never written down. (3) Attack fragmentation: enable expandable segments and re-measure reserved-vs-allocated drift before touching anything numerics-related. (4) Only then consider KV quantization or a smaller KV dtype, behind a quality gate. (5) Add replicas last -- horizontal scale hides an unbounded per-replica peak and the same failure returns at the next traffic-mix shift.

Design conclusion: the durable fix is an explicit admissible-set definition -- (max_model_len, max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens) chosen so the worst admissible concurrent set fits in device memory with a stated headroom fraction -- enforced at the router, plus a KV-pool sizing derived from that contract instead of from a leftover-memory fraction. Measured facts (allocator snapshots, scheduler counters) must be kept separate from estimates (the KV byte formula above is an estimate until validated against the observed high-water mark). No platform-specific claim should be made about a particular engine's default values without reading that deployment's actual config.

Rollback gate. Promote the change only if OOM per 1000 requests drops to zero across all three runs of arm B AND p99 TTFT regresses by less than 15% versus the arm-A baseline on the same frozen trace. Revert immediately if p99 TTFT regresses more than 15%, if throughput drops more than 10%, or if preemption/recompute counts rise enough to push TPOT past its SLO. Any quantization mitigation is gated separately on a task-level quality check, not on perplexity alone, because KV quantization degrades long-context retrieval before it moves aggregate perplexity.

Enabling KV-cache or weight quantization as an incident mitigation silently changes numerics; without a task-level quality gate this trades an availability incident for an undetected accuracy regression

GPU allocated and reserved bytes sampled at >=1 Hz spanning the failure, plus a CUDA caching-allocator snapshot taken at the failure boundary
Engine scheduler counters at failure time: KV blocks in use vs total, running and waiting sequence counts, preemption and recompute counts, prefix-cache hit rate

nvidia-smi per-process memory confirming no co-resident tenant, LoRA adapter, or draft model is consuming device memory unaccounted for

Design framing (variant 37). Treat this not as an incident to silence but as a missing capacity contract in the serving design. The system currently admits requests whose aggregate memory demand is unbounded, so the failure mode is structural.

Assumptions stated explicitly, because the priority ranking is only valid under them: single-node inference engine with a paged KV cache; static weights loaded once; CUDA caching allocator; no other tenant on the same GPUs; error is a CUDA out-of-memory from the device allocator rather than a host RSS OOM-kill. Any of these being false changes the ranking and the diagnosis must be re-derived rather than patched.

Mechanism. Steady-state GPU memory = model weights + CUDA/NCCL context and communication buffers + framework runtime buffers + activation peak of the largest scheduled batch + KV-cache pool. Only the last two scale with concurrency, which is exactly why the failure is intermittent: a deterministic sizing bug would fail on request one. KV bytes = 2 (K and V) * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * total_tokens; with GQA/MQA the kv_heads term is small, so context length and concurrent sequence count dominate, not attention-head count. If the engine preallocates a paged KV pool, genuine KV exhaustion should surface as preemption, recompute or queueing -- not as a CUDA OOM. An actual OOM therefore points outside the pool: transient activation peaks during prefill of long prompts (chunked prefill disabled or chunk size too large), caching-allocator fragmentation from mixed-size prefill buffers, or an unaccounted co-resident consumer (LoRA adapters, speculative draft model, logits/logprobs buffers proportional to batch x vocab, a second process sharing the device).

Null result that kills H1: OOM still occurs at the same trace offset with prefill capped, or the KV high-water mark reaches 100% before the failure. Competing hypothesis H2 (allocator fragmentation): reserved-minus-allocated bytes grow monotonically over hours and OOM occurs while reserved headroom exists; discriminated by an allocator snapshot at the failure boundary and by whether expandable_segments or a periodic empty_cache changes time-to-failure.
